text: In an emergency, one person shouldn't have
to make five calls.
What if one calm conversation could coordinate
the next steps?
Meet Ek Awaaz.
A voice-first assistant with a simple idea:
let the caller speak.
Let the system handle the coordination.
Here's the actual app.
A clear starting point, a live console,
and an incident report.
Let's walk through a simulated road accident.
Listen, understand, confirm, coordinate.
Here's how it works.
The caller speaks naturally, in Hinglish.
A bike accident, with two people injured.
Their words appear in the live transcript.
Key details are highlighted as they arrive.
One conversation, turning into a shared picture.
Beside the transcript, the incident card takes
shape. Location, people, and severity come together.
Watch the address update when the caller
gives a correction.
The latest information matters more than the
first guess.
The caller confirms the incident type and
location before coordination begins.
See that checkpoint on the timeline?
Understanding comes before action.
Now the work splits.
The listener supports the conversation.
The dispatcher handles the next steps in
parallel.
In this recorded demo, ambulance and family
outreach are simulated, with a location link
shown alongside them.
Each step has a visible status, so
you can follow the handoff instead of
wondering what's happening behind the scenes.
When speaking freely isn't possible, the interaction
changes. Silent mode offers discreet prompts and
keypad responses.
Less pressure on the caller, with a
clear path to the next step.
The incident report brings details and timestamped
actions together.
This is a prototype, not a live
emergency response.
No public emergency service was contacted.
Every step stays visible.
Ek Awaaz.
One voice, many calls.
Built with Bolna.
